data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The night-time UHI is governed by the urban sky view factor: deep street canyons trap longwave radiation and slow radiative cooling; the gap scales with building height and built density, which reduce the effective view of the cold sky.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a city has very low building height or open morphology, the sky view factor approaches the rural value and the trapping effect weakens.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If atmospheric humidity or cloud cover is high, longwave cooling is already suppressed in both city and countryside, reducing the sky-view effect.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If thermal mass or anthropogenic heat dominates, sky view factor is not the single best explanatory mechanism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"On a clear night, radiative cooling to the cold sky is a primary heat sink; tall, dense buildings obstruct the sky view, reradiating longwave radiation back to the surface and slowing the urban cooling rate; cities with deeper canyons and lower sky view factors exhibit a larger nocturnal UHI.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
